# The Titan Beacon Chain

On Titan's Shoal Point, keeper Noor Adeyemi has fourteen months left on an eighteen-month contract that requires her to acknowledge, log, and never silence a single distress call — even the one now arriving in her own voice, reporting a position she never gave. The station's clear-sky relay window opens once every sixteen days; the rest of the time, everything on Kraken Mare's sea-lanes routes through cache satellites nineteen years frozen and unable to tell a live signal from a replayed one. The calls keep coming, each stamped further ahead of station time than the last, and when Noor does the arithmetic on the drift, it points backward — to a forty-one-second gap in her own power log, and further still, to the final entries of Emlen Pryce, the predecessor who died at this beacon and was convicted, after the fact and on evidence months late, of abandoning it. Bound by a Convention that treats every acknowledged distress as gospel and forbids a keeper from ever going dark, Noor cannot simply refuse the call. She has twelve seconds each way to prove what she suspects before a barge under way in weather minima changes course for coordinates that may be nothing but her own voice, echoing forward through machinery that was never built to know the difference between rescue and repetition. A hard-science procedural about instruments, law, and the last data you can trust.

**For readers of:** *The Martian*, *Version Control*, *Rendezvous with Rama*

---

# Chapter 1 — Forty-One Seconds

Noor Adeyemi woke at 15:20 into the tail of the blackout, which was the only part of a magnetopause passage that ever felt like weather. Five hours predicted, five hours delivered, the ionosphere shrugging under the solar wind while the log room hissed with nothing. She lay a moment in the bunk alcove and listened to the heat exchanger, which was the loudest thing at Shoal Point, and to the methane drizzle on the roof, which was the second.

The alternation had slipped again. She could tell before she looked, because the room was warm in the way that meant the heaters had been given the whole of the two radioisotope units for longer than their forty minutes. Six hundred watts electrical, continuous, plus whatever the genset's oxidiser would bear, and the radar's forty kilowatts of pulse came out of the genset or came out of nothing. She threw the alternation back by hand at the panel, radar up, heaters down, and stood in her liner suit with her arms crossed while the pulse count climbed and steadied.

Then the tally sheet, because the checklist said tally sheet.

Oxidiser at six percent. She wrote it in the column in her own small upright hand, and the line above hers was still Emlen Pryce's, sixteen months old, a figure and then a annotation and then a smaller annotation on the annotation, the ink of a man who had never met a number he trusted to stand alone. The Authority had never sent a fresh sheet. She had stopped expecting one.

At 15:40 the first clear relay pass came over and the cache emptied itself into Beacon Eleven.

In the blind half nothing reached the surface unrelayed; for eight days out of every sixteen, Titan's locked face turned away and everything she knew arrived as stored packets from the Relay Trust's satellites. So she was used to traffic arriving in a lump. She was not used to the inbound alert, and she was not used to what came out of the speaker when she crossed the room and let it play.

It was a distress call. It carried Beacon Eleven's station hash — her hash, her pulse signature, the Authority's proof of presence.

And it was her voice. Not like her voice. Hers: flat, the phrase-bank cadence of a commissioning booth at Enceladus, the numerals clipped and spaced the way a machine spaces numerals it has been handed one at a time. It gave a position report. She had never made that position report in her life.

She looked at the clock. Then she looked at the clock again, because she trusted the clock further than she trusted herself, and the packet timestamp had not changed: one hour and eighteen minutes ahead of station time.

The station had already acknowledged it. Automatically, at receipt, per stored procedure, and forwarded it on, before she had finished crossing four metres of floor.

She sat down and logged it verbatim, with the local timestamp, exactly as the Convention required, and added no interpretation, because interpretation was not hers to add. Then she wrote one further line: that she could not power down the beacon to think about it. A lit beacon was not hers to darken. Abandonment was tried on Enceladus, on evidence months late.

Outside, the drizzle went on. The heat exchanger went on. She sat with her own voice on the log and waited for the next pass.

# Chapter 2 — Divide by Seventy-Eight

The second copy came down at 04:44 on Contract Day 423, and it was not a second copy. It was the same one. Same hash, same waveform, her voice saying *Beacon Eleven, keeper reports* with the flat booth cadence of a woman reading phrases off a card in a room on Enceladus. Only the stamp had moved: 2:36 ahead of station time now, where yesterday it had been 1:18.

She wrote it out verbatim, because that was the law, and then she wrote the two offsets in a column in the margin, which was not.

The third arrived on the pass after that, at 3:54. Three numbers, evenly spaced. She did the subtraction twice and got seventy-eight both times, and sat with the pen not moving, because seventy-eight was not an arbitrary number on Titan this season. Seventy-eight minutes was Earth, one way. It was the number printed on the header of every packet she had sent in fourteen months.

The relay was adding the Earth correction. Then handling the packet again and adding it again. Nothing in the firmware said *already done*; nothing in the firmware needed to, until a packet came round twice. The offset was not a timestamp at all. It was a count of how many times the cache had touched the thing.

Which left the other half of it, and the other half was worse. The cache ran six hours deep. Nothing could loiter in it from one day's pass to the next — the packet should have aged out and died before breakfast on 422. It had not aged out because it had never sat still. Her own station had taken it in as an inbound distress and done what the Convention required of a keeper: log verbatim, acknowledge, forward. The forwarded copy dropped straight back into the cache as a fresh arrival, with a fresh arrival time, and six hours of depth can never expire a thing that keeps arriving. Beacon Eleven was not haunted. Beacon Eleven was renewing the subscription, every pass, by the book.

So she divided. Three cycles at seventy-eight minutes, counted back across the passes, and the arithmetic set her down at 04:12 on Contract Day 422, eleven hours before she had ever heard the call.

The power log was in the drawer where the power log always was. She ran her finger down the alternation column to 04:12 and found the slip she had already corrected and already forgotten: radar unpowered, forty-one seconds, heaters holding. Forty-one seconds of Beacon Eleven not pulsing. The dead-man watchdog had done exactly what it was built to do — spoken a position report in the keeper's voice, because a keeper who cannot speak still has a voice on file, 312 phrases and a numeral set, recorded in ninety minutes and never thought about since.

The call from her future was a receipt for a gap she had slept through.

She sent the query up to Jun Halloran at the Relay Trust anyway, and a pass and a half later the answer came back cached and stale: cache behaviour was proprietary; Rev 6.2 had operated to specification for nineteen years. It read like a lie. She decided it was a muzzle, which was worse, because a muzzle meant he had nothing to add.

The archive locker was cold and smelled of dry ice-dust. Pryce's final nine entries were in his own hand, annotated in his own margins, the way a man annotates himself when there is nobody else to check him.

*1:18.* Then *2:36.* Then *3:54.* Then, two entries later, without emphasis: *The cache keeps things.*

The ninth entry logged an inbound distress. Keeper down, coordinates on the ice apron. He had acknowledged it, because the Convention said acknowledge, and noted the suit check, and the time he went out.

Somebody else's handwriting closed the log nine days later. Iver Brekke's abandonment verdict was filed behind it in the same folder, correct on every page, and wrong.

# Chapter 3 — Human-Acknowledged

Contract Day 424, 09:41. The call came in her own voice, and it was calm the way she was calm on a checklist: keeper down, shoal ice, forty kilometres offshore, bearing 013. She listened to herself say a coordinate she had never transmitted and watched the header strip come up empty where the station hash belonged. No hash. No pulse count. Underneath it, riding as a payload block, a commissioning fragment sixteen months old with Emlen Pryce's station identity burned into it like a fingerprint on cold glass.

*Tammuz* answered the relay four minutes later. Six hours out, wind at the top of her band, already below Convention minima on Consortium orders — and altering course, because the Convention does not let a master weigh a distress call against her own draught.

Shoal ice at forty kilometres would put the barge aground in weather nobody would audit until spring.

Noor did not use the relay. Anything she gave the cache it would keep, and re-emit, and keep again. She went to the radar band direct, 3 cm, twelve seconds each way, and she spent an hour reducing it to one sentence a barge master could act on inside a single exchange.

"*Tammuz*, Beacon Eleven. A real distress from this station carries a live hash and a rising pulse count. That call carries a dead man's. Hold your course."

Twelve seconds out. Twelve back. Okonkwo's voice came through the drizzle-hiss with no hedging in it at all: *Holding. Log it that I took a beacon's word over my charter's.*

On the same band, unlogged and unlicensed, something else was listening. At 14:20 an aerostat return lifted north out of the shoal margin at forty knots and stopped answering the interrogator. Noor wrote the bearing into the log, 013 to 358, climbing, no name attached, because she could not prove one and a log that guesses is worth nothing at an audit.

Contract Day 425, 02:07. She could not power down; that was the offence, and the watchdog would only fire again in the dark. She could not ignore a distress; the Convention forbade it. The loop lived on automation, and Rev 6.2 would re-forward anything not flagged human-acknowledged — a flag no machine was permitted to set.

So she keyed the microphone and answered herself.

"Beacon Eleven, Shoal Point. Keeper Noor Adeyemi acknowledging, live, by voice, station identity confirmed lit."

The cache took it and did not give it back. By 05:00 the queue was empty.

Contract Day 427. Line of sight to Earth returned at 11:52. She assembled the log verbatim — the forty-one seconds dark, timestamped, the arithmetic of the offsets, Pryce's nine entries appended whole — and added no argument to it. Iver Brekke would not hear it for seventy-eight minutes, could not reply in under two hours thirty-six, and would not rule for months.

The packet went out. The beacon stayed lit.
